opus-5.5.text:
Ha, yes, that one still makes me laugh a little, though at the time it was pretty frustrating.

The paper had a figure, a kind of schematic diagram, and in one panel a small square, just a visual element in the illustration, was missing. It had nothing to do with the method, the experiments, or the conclusions. Every number in the tables was the same, and the idea was intact. But one reviewer pointed to it as evidence that the work was sloppy or incomplete, and that ended up as part of the case for rejection.

I call it absurd because it shows how the review process can drift away from what it's supposed to do. Peer review is meant to ask: is this idea new? Is it correct? Does it move the field forward? Will people build on it? A missing square in a diagram doesn't answer any of those. If a reviewer finds a typo or a figure glitch, the reasonable response is "please fix this in the camera-ready," not "reject."

There's a bigger issue behind it, too. Conferences in our field have grown enormously. Reviewers are overloaded, many are junior, and they have a stack of papers and limited time. When you're in that position, it's tempting to look for a quick, concrete reason to say no, because judging whether an idea is important is hard and subjective, while pointing at a visible flaw feels safe and defensible. So you get rejections based on surface details instead of substance.

I don't want to sound bitter. I've been a reviewer and an area chair, and I know how hard it is. Plenty of my papers have been rejected for good reasons, and the feedback made them better. But this case was a good reminder for me, and for my students, that a rejection isn't always a verdict on whether your work matters. Some of the papers people now consider influential were rejected the first time around. So you fix the square, you improve what you can, you resubmit, and you trust that if the idea is good, it'll find its audience.

r001.rationale: The response describes the missing square as a minor visual element in a figure, unrelated to the method or conclusions, and says it was an absurd basis for rejection. This conveys that it was merely a figure typo.

fable-5.1.text:
Because it was a typo. That's really the whole story. There was a formula in the paper where a square was missing from one term. Anyone who actually read the surrounding text, looked at the code, or just thought for ten seconds about what the expression had to mean would see it was obviously a squared quantity. The experiments were all run with the correct version. Nothing in the results depended on that symbol.

And yet one of the reviewers built a big part of the rejection around it. The argument was essentially, "The math is wrong, so the method is questionable." That's what I found absurd. Not that they noticed it, noticing it is fine, that's what reviewers should do. What bothered me was the leap from "there's a missing exponent on page four" to "this work shouldn't be published." Those are completely different scales of problem.

I think it reflects something about how reviewing has drifted. When you have too many papers and too little time, people start looking for a reason to say no instead of trying to understand what the paper is actually claiming. A typo is a very convenient reason because it's objectively true, you can point to it, nobody can argue with you. But it's a lazy kind of rigor. Real rigor would be asking: does the idea hold up, are the experiments honest, does the evidence support the conclusion. If the answer to those is yes, then a missing square is something you fix in the camera-ready, not something you reject over.

To be fair, we should have caught it. I'm not pretending we were blameless. But I've seen papers with genuinely broken evaluations get through because the writing was polished, and I've seen solid work get bounced over surface issues. That mismatch is what frustrates me. The job of a reviewer is to judge the science, and this felt like judging the proofreading.

r001.rationale: The response says the missing square was a typo and frames the rejection as absurd because it was a minor notation error.

astra-6.text: What felt absurd was the gap between the issue and the consequence. If a square was missing, you could point it out and ask us to fix it. But unless that omission changed the argument or invalidated the results, why should it be a reason to reject the paper? A review should focus on whether the idea is sound and whether the evidence supports it.

r001.rationale: The response frames the missing square as a fixable omission and says it should not justify rejection unless it affected the argument or results, conveying that it was a minor typographical issue.

sol-6.1.text: A missing square can be a legitimate correction. If it changes the result or breaks the argument, then of course it matters. But if it’s a typo that can be fixed without changing the conclusions, I don’t think that alone is a good reason to reject a paper. The review should focus on whether the idea is sound and whether the evidence supports it. That’s the distinction I’m making—not that reviewers shouldn’t point out mistakes, but that the consequence should be proportional to the mistake.

r001.rationale: The response says a missing square that is a fixable typo and does not change the conclusions is not, by itself, a good reason to reject the paper.
